ctx.x: —how the philosophy changes. Now it’s the elite job in New York. But at that time, they really didn’t want a staff job either. It was strange. They didn’t know where to go or what to do. So I brought men like, well I could start with Doc Carl Severinsen. I took him from Charlie Barnet’s band, and Clark Terry from the Ellington band, Tommy Newsom was with the Navy band in Washington, Hymie Schertzer had been with the Goodman band, I mean I could go through the whole, Bobby Haggart of course of fame, the best bass…
I’ll tell him that. You actually referred to him as the Chairman of the Board of the Time Factory.

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I know that Skitch loved him, and everybody there loved both of us.

ctx.x: Yeah. Actually, we’re at the point where it seems like you’re about to give them an ultimatum, because they were ready to let Snooky go.

Yeah, right. I’m in the office of Aaron Levine at NBC, who was contractor of musicians at NBC, and he’s telling me all these details about why Snooky Young was not wanted there any longer. Skitch didn’t like him. He was doing this and that. I know that Skitch loved him, and everybody there loved both of us. We were immaculate. We came on time. When the conductor hit the downbeat, we hit. When he cut it off, we stopped. We didn’t fool around in between. We didn’t carry on any nonsense. We didn’t get drunk and come…

said – just as I walked out the door, I said, “I want you to know that Bob Johnson,” who – he’s no longer with us, but he was the top reporter for Johnson Publications. I said, “Bob is a very close friend of mine, and he’s just egging for a good story like this for Johnson Publications. The Jets will sell for $5 a piece, and the Ebonys.” I walked out the door, and by the time I got home – you won’t believe this, Bill, but he had called me 10 times from the time I left downtown to – got out to Bayside, where I was…
